Now record the landscape. Let me construct a taxonomy:

Field: Temporal / time-aware retrieval-augmented QA over evolving documents.

Categories:
1. Temporal QA datasets & benchmarks (parent: none) — paper_ids: arxiv:2109.06157 (SituatedQA), doi:10.2139/ssrn.7174868 (TemporalESG), doi:10.3390/sym18091498 (TempFinQA), arxiv:2505.20243 (survey of them)
   - Sub: Web/open-domain temporal QA benchmarks — arxiv:2109.06157
   - Sub: Domain temporal benchmarks (ESG, finance, regulatory) — doi:10.2139/ssrn.7174868, doi:10.3390/sym18091498, doi:10.2139/ssrn.7087840
2. Temporal retrieval mechanisms (parent none):
   - 2a. Graded temporal decay / recency weighting — doi:10.2139/ssrn.7174868 (exponential decay), doi:10.1109/iri69576.2026.00090 (learnable exponential decay)
   - 2b. Hard as-of / validity-interval filtering — doi:10.3390/sym18091498
   - 2c. Timestamp-aware embeddings/representation learning — doi:10.1109/iri69576.2026.00090 (Layer 1), doi:10.1109/bigdata66926.2025.11402566 (temporal-aware RAG, title-only)
   - 2d. Temporal query decomposition / iterative retrieval (survey-mentioned systems: TimeR4, TimeRAG, TempRALM) — arxiv:2505.20243 (as reviewed, not primary papers)
3. Reader-side temporal reasoning (parent none) — doi:10.18653/v1/2023.findings-emnlp.67 (temporal graph fusion), doi:10.18653/v1/2024.findings-emnlp.848 (embedding + contrastive RL)
4. Static retrieval baselines on regulatory documents (parent none) — doi:10.2139/ssrn.7087840

Proposed idea position: at the intersection of category 2a (graded temporal relevance) and 2b (validity), applied to a domain (amended statutes/regulations) currently occupied by category 4 (static regulatory retrieval) and adjacent to category 1's domain benchmarks; framed as a retrieval-agnostic re-ranking layer (not covered by any category, since 2a/2b are implemented inside fixed architectures).

Dominant approaches: dense/semantic retrieval as the default; hybrid lexical+dense; explicit temporal decay as the temporal fix; as-of hard filtering; timestamp-conditioned embeddings; reader-side temporal graph fusion / temporal RL.

Common assumptions: timestamps or as-of dates are available and reliable; temporal relevance decreases with age (recency = validity); base/corpus is static or updated by snapshot replacement; a single document timestamp suffices for all statements in it; answer accuracy or retrieval precision is the target metric.

Common datasets: none shared widely; SituatedQA, TimeQA (web QA), TemporalESG (ESG), TempFinQA (SEC filings), ICEWS14/TimE (TKG/clinical), RMA central bank reports (regulatory, static).

Common benchmarks: SituatedQA, TimeQA, TemporalESG, TempFinQA, TimE, RMA RAG benchmark.

Common metrics: answer accuracy/EM-F1, temporal accuracy, entity precision, recall, ROUGE/BERTScore/faithfulness, temporal evidence leakage, hallucination rate, retrieval precision.

Repeated limitations:
- Temporal benchmarks are domain-specific and none target amended statutes with near-duplicate versions (papers: arxiv:2505.20243, doi:10.2139/ssrn.7174868, doi:10.3390/sym18091498, doi:10.2139/ssrn.7087840)
- Temporal signal equated with recency/decay while legal validity can be non-monotone (papers: doi:10.1109/iri69576.2026.00090, doi:10.2139/ssrn.7174868 vs doi:10.3390/sym18091498)
- Methods are architecture-specific rather than retrieval-agnostic (papers: doi:10.1109/iri69576.2026.00090, doi:10.2139/ssrn.7174868); hmm "repeated across papers" — I'd say methods couple temporal handling to a specific pipeline; supported by both.
- Static corpora in regulatory/legal QA (papers: arxiv:2505.20243, doi:10.2139/ssrn.7087840)
- Evaluation lacks temporal-correctness metric beyond answer accuracy in some works (SituatedQA, Fusing Temporal Graphs metrics "not stated"). Maybe.

Underexplored combinations:
- Retrieval-agnostic temporal re-ranking applied post hoc to arbitrary retrievers (none of the analyzed works does this)
- Amended statutes/regulations with near-duplicate successive versions + validity intervals + time-stamped queries
- Combining hard validity-interval filtering with graded semantic+temporal scoring (contrast 2a vs 2b) in one framework
- Evaluating version-confusion/temporal contamination on legal text (metric exists in finance as temporal evidence leakage)
- Separating document-creation time from event/validity time (survey flags this mismatch as failure mode) in legal corpora
- Interaction with sparse retrievers on regulatory text (RMA shows BM25 beats hybrid on multihop)

Contradictions:
- Graded temporal decay (recency = relevance) vs hard as-of validity boundary: Bridging + Chronofy vs TempFinRAG; the survey warns recency bias is a failure mode. Papers: doi:10.2139/ssrn.7174868, doi:10.1109/iri69576.2026.00090 vs doi:10.3390/sym18091498, arxiv:2505.20243.
- Sparse vs hybrid on regulatory/multihop: RMA finds BM25 > hybrid on multihop, while the same paper finds hybrid best overall; TemporalESG finds hybrid three-signal best. Papers: doi:10.2139/ssrn.7087840 vs doi:10.2139/ssrn.7174868.
- Fine-tuning/representation learning vs architectural fix: Bridging says fine-tuning gives only marginal gains (structural problem), while Enhancing Temporal Sensitivity reports significant gains from embedding+RL. Papers: doi:10.2139/ssrn.7174868 vs doi:10.18653/v1/2024.findings-emnlp.848.

That last is a nice contradiction.

input.field_name: Time-aware retrieval-augmented question answering over evolving, time-stamped and versioned documents

categories.description: Resources that pair time-dependent questions with an explicit temporal context or target date.
categories.name: Temporal QA benchmarks and datasets

categories.description: Datasets built from web or open-retrieval QA where answers drift with the question's date (e.g., SituatedQA, TimeQA).
categories.name: Web / open-domain temporal QA benchmarks

categories.description: Domain-specific corpora with time-stamped or as-of queries: ESG disclosures, SEC filings, central-bank reports.
categories.name: Domain temporal benchmarks (ESG, financial, regulatory)

categories.description: Methods that change which evidence is retrieved depending on time, rather than only how it is read.
categories.name: Temporal retrieval mechanisms

categories.description: Temporal relevance decays with elapsed time (exponential decay, learnable decay coefficients), treating recency as validity.
categories.name: Graded temporal decay / recency weighting

categories.description: Evidence is admitted only if publicly available / in force at the query's as-of date, a binary temporal boundary rather than a graded score.
categories.name: Hard as-of / validity-interval filtering

categories.description: Time is encoded into embeddings or model parameters (temporal subspaces, timestamp-conditioned encoders) instead of the ranking score.
categories.name: Timestamp-aware representation learning

categories.description: Retrieval pipelines that decompose underspecified temporal queries and re-retrieve/re-rank with explicit time anchors (e.g., TimeR4, TimeRAG, TempRALM, as reviewed by the survey).
categories.name: Iterative / decomposed temporal RAG

categories.description: Approaches that leave retrieval unchanged and improve the reader's ability to reason over times (temporal graph fusion, temporal-aware embeddings plus contrastive RL).
categories.name: Reader-side temporal reasoning

categories.description: Sparse, dense and hybrid retrieval benchmarks and systems over regulatory documents with no temporal dimension (no target dates, no versions).
categories.name: Static document retrieval over regulatory / legal corpora

categories.description: Work that catalogues tasks, datasets and open challenges without proposing a method or benchmark.
categories.name: Temporal QA surveys and meta-analysis

common_assumptions: A usable timestamp, version date or as-of date is available for every document/passage and for every query
Temporal relevance is monotone in age: older evidence is less valid (recency-as-validity), so decay is the natural temporal signal
A single document-level timestamp adequately represents all statements in the document
The corpus is either static (no versioning) or updated by snapshot replacement, not by tracking amendments to the same text
Answer accuracy or retrieval precision is the target quantity, so temporal correctness is instrumental rather than measured directly (except where temporal accuracy / leakage is reported)
The temporal remedy is usually implemented inside one specific pipeline (fixed hybrid, graph retrieval, multimodal verifier) rather than as a component transferable across retrievers
common_datasets: SituatedQA (9K questions from four open-retrieval QA datasets)
RMA Bhutan payment system reports (static regulatory corpus)
Legal QA datasets (reviewed; reported as static)
dominant_approaches: Dense semantic retrieval as the default evidence selector, with BM25 and hybrid lexical+dense as baselines
Explicit temporal decay (usually exponential) multiplied into or learned within retrieval scores
Hard as-of or availability boundaries that filter evidence by date
Timestamp-conditioned or temporally-augmented embeddings and contrastive/reinforcement training
Reader-side temporal graph construction and fusion
Temporal query decomposition and iterative retrieve-rerank pipelines
Domain benchmark construction with manually validated temporal queries
input.idea_position: The idea sits at the intersection of 'Temporal retrieval mechanisms' (it adopts a graded temporal relevance/decay signal of the kind in the graded-decay sub-category, while the correctness argument depends on the hard as-of validity notion in the other sub-category) and 'Domain temporal benchmarks' — but the domain it targets, continuously amended statutes/regulations with near-duplicate successive versions and validity intervals, is currently served only by the 'Static document retrieval over regulatory/legal corpora' category. Its distinctive placement is as a retrieval-agnostic re-ranking layer that can be attached to any base retriever; every existing temporal-retrieval category instead couples temporal handling to one specific architecture or pipeline, so the plug-in form plus the amended-statute setting is the unoccupied position.

repeated_limitations.description: No existing benchmark targets continuously amended statutes/regulations with near-duplicate successive versions, validity metadata and time-stamped queries; the closest temporal benchmarks are ESG disclosures, financial filings and date-annotated web QA, while regulatory-document work is static.
Temporal relevance is operationalised as recency/decay, which is unjustified when the authoritative text is the version in force at the target date and a superseded clause can be temporally nearest.
Temporal handling is coupled to a specific pipeline (three-signal hybrid, graph retrieval with learned decay, multimodal verifier), so transfer to an arbitrary base retriever is not demonstrated.
Regulatory and legal retrieval resources lack any temporal dimension: questions carry no target date and corpora are treated as static.

Some evaluations report only end-task answer quality, so temporal correctness of the retrieved evidence is not isolated (e.g., SituatedQA and the temporal-graph fusion work report no temporal-contamination metric).

contradictions.description: Graded temporal decay (recency = validity) versus hard as-of validity: the three-signal hybrid and Chronofy multiply retrieval by exponential decay, whereas TempFinRAG enforces a binary availability boundary and requires 'asymmetric access across time'; the survey independently warns that temporal retrieval fails due to 'recency bias'. These cannot both be right for amended normative text.

Whether the temporal fix is architectural or trainable: the temporal-semantic benchmark paper reports that fine-tuning on 7,000+ temporal examples yields only marginal gains because the limitation is structural, while the TSQA reasoning paper reports significant gains from temporal-aware embeddings plus contrastive reinforcement learning.

Sparse versus hybrid retrieval on regulatory text: one regulatory benchmark finds hybrid best overall but BM25 better on multihop queries, while the temporal hybrid framework reports a large advantage for the combined lexical+dense+decay signal; the optimal base retriever for regulatory multi-document reasoning is therefore unsettled.

underexplored_combinations: A retrieval-agnostic temporal re-ranking term evaluated across multiple base retrievers (sparse, dense, hybrid) on the same corpus — no analyzed work does this
Amended statutes/regulations with near-duplicate successive versions, explicit validity intervals (in-force start/end), and time-stamped queries as a benchmark
Combining a hard validity-interval as-of filter with a graded semantic+temporal score in one framework, so that validity bounds the candidate set while semantic-temporal similarity ranks within it
Measuring version confusion / temporal contamination (superseded or not-yet-in-force clause retrieved) on legal text, adapting the temporal-evidence-leakage metric from financial point-in-time QA
Separating document/version timestamp from the validity period of the clause text itself, since the survey flags document-creation-time versus event-time mismatch as a failure mode
Retrieval-agnostic temporal re-ranking over sparse BM25, given evidence that BM25 can beat hybrid on multi-document regulatory queries
Benchmarking on jurisdiction-scale statute corpora (e.g., amendment-tracked codes) rather than corporate disclosures, where supersession chains are long and dense

input.description: Every retrieved temporal-retrieval method implements the temporal signal inside a specific pipeline (a fixed three-signal hybrid, graph-based retrieval with learned decay, or a multimodal verifier). The proposal's only architectural novelty claim is that the same signal can be added to any standard retriever as a post-hoc re-ranking term. If that transfer is trivial or yields no additional benefit over the fixed hybrid, the 'retrieval-agnostic' framing adds little; if base-retriever choice materially interacts with the temporal term, the framing is a substantive contribution.
input.question: Is 'retrieval-agnostic' a substantive contribution, or does the temporal relevance term reduce to an already-published fixed hybrid, making the plug-in framing a repackaging with little added value?
input.rationale: Landscape shows the temporal mechanism is covered in architecture-specific systems with no cross-retriever transfer study, and the regulatory benchmark shows hybrid is not uniformly best (BM25 wins on multihop), suggesting base-retriever interaction is real but untested.

input.resolution: Partially resolved by analysis: the mechanism (semantic retrieval plus explicit temporal decay) and the benchmark-construction pattern are already published in adjacent domains — a three-signal BM25+dense+exponential-decay hybrid with a 970-query temporal benchmark, and learnable exponential decay inside graph-based retrieval. However, no analyzed work (a) attaches the temporal term to an arbitrary base retriever, (b) targets amended statutes/regulations with near-duplicate successive versions and validity intervals, or (c) measures version confusion on legal text. So the core mechanism is pre-empted while the specific instantiation remains unoccupied; this must be stress-tested against work not yet retrieved before any novelty claim.
